I say: its benefit is that His saying 'there is no god but He' is affirmation of oneness (tawḥīd), and His saying 'upholding justice' is affirmation of equity; so when He follows it with His saying {إِنَّ الدِّينَ عِندَ الله الإسلام}, He announces that Islam is justice and oneness, and it is the religion with Allah, and whatever is other than it is nothing of religion in His sight."

As for al-Kisāʾī's reading, it has several views. The first: that it is a badal (substitute) for «أنه لا إله إلا هو» according to the reading of the majority in «أنه لا إله إلا هو», and in this there are two views. The first: that it is a badal of the thing for the thing (badal al-shayʾ min al-shayʾ), in that the religion, which is Islam, includes justice and oneness and is the same in meaning. The second: that it is badal ishtimāl (inclusion substitute), because Islam includes oneness and justice.

The second of the earlier views: that «أنَّ الدين» is a badal of His saying «قائماً بالقسط». Then you have two considerations. The first: you make it a badal of its wording, so the position of «أنَّ الدين» is genitive. The second: you make it a badal of its place, so its position is accusative. This second has no need, although Abū l-Baqāʾ mentioned it. The badal is sound in meaning only because the religion, which is Islam, is equity and justice, so this too is a badal of the thing for the thing, the two being one and the same; and it may be badal ishtimāl, because religion includes equity, which is justice. These analyses are from Abū ʿAlī al-Fārisī, and al-Zamakhsharī followed him in some of them. The Shaykh said: "Abū ʿAlī was a Muʿtazilite, and so his speech includes the Muʿtazilite expressions of justice and oneness." I (al-Samīn) say: who among the Sunnis turns away from oneness and justice, such that it would be specific to the Muʿtazila? Rather he saw these words frequently in al-Zamakhsharī's speech, and in his view he is a Muʿtazilite, so whoever speaks of oneness and justice is, in his view, a Muʿtazilite.

Then he said: "On the badal from «أنه», he and others have analyzed it, but it is not good, because it leads to a construction so remote that its like would not occur in the speech of the Arabs, namely: 'Zayd knew that there is no brave man but he, and Banū Dārim, meeting wars, no brave man but he, the champion, the protector, that the praiseworthy quality is valour.' And a closer approximation of this example: 'Zayd struck ʿĀʾisha and the two ʿUmars, being furious, your sister', where «furious» is a ḥāl from Zayd, and «your sister» is a badal of ʿĀʾisha; so there is separation between the badal and what it substitutes for by a conjunction, which is not permissible, and by a ḥāl for other than what is substituted for, which is not permissible, because a stranger intervenes between the badal and what it substitutes for." End of quotation.

His saying "Zayd knew" is parallel to «شهد الله»; and his saying "that there is no brave man but he" parallels «أنه لا إله إلا هو». And his saying "and Banū Dārim" parallels «والملائكة». And his saying "meeting wars" parallels «قائماً بالقسط»; and his saying "no brave man but he" parallels "there is no god but He", so he brought it repeated as in the verse; and his saying "the champion, the protector" parallels «العزيز الحكيم»; and his saying "that the praiseworthy quality is valour" parallels {إِنَّ الدِّينَ عِندَ الله الإسلام}. It is not clear to me that there is any prohibition of this or unsoundness of its construction such that he should say "not good" and "it is remote that the like of it would come from the Arabs." And what he claimed in the second example, that there is separation by a stranger, needs consideration, since these sentences have all become like one sentence because of what they include of the strengthening of words by one another; and Abū ʿAlī, Abū l-Qāsim (al-Zamakhsharī) and others were not in the position of people ignorant of the soundness or corruption of the construction of some speech.

Then the Shaykh said: "Al-Zamakhsharī said: 'They were also read with both fatḥa, on the basis that the second is a badal of the first, as if it were said: "Allah bore witness that the religion with Allah is Islam"; and the badal is the thing substituted for in meaning, so it is a clear explanation, because the religion of Islam is oneness and justice.'" He said: "This is a transmission of Abū ʿAlī's speech without completeness."

The third of the views: that «أنَّ الدينَ» is conjoined to «أنه لا إله إلا هو», with the conjunction omitted from it. Ibn Jarīr said this, and Ibn ʿAṭiyya weakened it, and did not explain the reason for its weakness.

The Shaykh said: "The reason for its weakness is that the construction is discordant with the implied conjunction, for there would be separation between the two nominative conjoined items by the accusative object, and between the two accusative conjoined items by the nominative, and by two parenthetical clauses; and the construction becomes like your saying: 'Zayd ate bread and ʿAmr fish', meaning you separated Zayd from ʿAmr by 'bread', and separated 'bread' from 'fish' by ʿAmr, whereas the original before the separation was 'Zayd and ʿAmr ate bread and fish'."

The fourth: that it is governed by His saying «شهد الله», that is: "Allah bore witness that the religion...", and when the preposition was dropped it was permissible to rule that its place is accusative or genitive. If you say: this analysis is only directed on the reading of Ibn ʿAbbās, which is kasra on the first inna, and the sentence is then parenthetical between «شهد» and its governed object, as I presented before; but on the reading with fatḥa on the first «أنَّ», which is the reading of the majority, what I mentioned of the analysis is not directed, because the first is governed by it and it is sufficed by it. The answer: that it is also directed with the fatḥa of the first, which is that you make the first on the omission of the lām of cause, its implied form being: "Allah bore witness that the religion with Allah is Islam because there is no god but He." This analysis kept nagging at my mind for a time, and I did not see that they had mentioned it, until I saw al-Wāḥidī mention it, and he said: "This is the meaning of al-Farrāʾ's saying where he argues for al-Kisāʾī: 'If you wish you may make «أنه» on the basis of the condition (sharṭ), and make the testimony fall upon His saying {إِنَّ الدِّينَ عِندَ الله الإسلام}, and the first «أنَّ» may take the genitive, as in your saying: "Allah bore witness to His oneness that the religion with Allah is Islam".'"

This is speech problematic in itself. The meaning of his saying "on the basis of the condition" is: the cause ('illa). He called the cause a condition because the conditioned depends on it, as the effect depends on its cause, so it is a cause; but it is contrary to the terminology of the grammarians.

Then al-Wāḥidī objected to this analysis, that if it were so, repeating the name of Allah would not be good, and the construction would have been «إنَّ الدين عنده الإسلام», since the name had already preceded, so the sound way is the pronoun. Then he answered that the Arabs sometimes repeat the name in place of the pronoun, and recited:

1206 - لا أَرَى الموتَ يَسْبِقُ الموتَ شيءٌ ... نَغَّصَ الموتُ ذا الغِنى والفقيرا
(I do not see anything outstripping death; death has spoiled life for the rich and the poor.)

meaning that it is a case of placing the overt noun in the place of the pronoun, and what adds to its goodness here is that it is in a place of glorification and magnification.

The fifth: that, on the omission of the preposition, it is governed by the word «الحكيم», as if it were said: "wise in that", that is: "the judge that"; so ḥakīm is a form of exaggeration converted from fāʿil, like ʿalīm, khabīr and baṣīr, that is, one exaggerating in these attributes. He departed from the word ḥākim to ḥakīm, with the additional exaggeration, to match «العزيز». The meaning of the exaggeration is the repetition of His judgement with respect to the laws that the religion with Allah is Islam, or that He judged in every law by that. This view was mentioned by the Shaykh, and it is as if it were his own analysis. Then he said: "If you ask: why did you take ḥakīm as converted from fāʿil to faʿīl for exaggeration, and why did you not make it faʿīl in the sense of mufʿil, so that it would be in the sense of muḥkim (one who makes firm), as they said: alīm in the sense of mūlim, and samīʿ in the sense of musmiʿ, from the saying of the poet:

1207 - أَمِنْ ريحانَةَ الداعي السميعُ ... . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . .
(Is it from Rayḥāna that the summoner, the hearer...?) [the second half-verse is elided in the source]

The answer is that we do not concede that faʿīl is in the sense of mufʿil, and alīm and samīʿ may be interpreted as other than mufʿil; and even if we concede that, it is so rare and anomalous that it cannot be taken as a norm, unlike faʿīl converted from fāʿil, which is very frequent and beyond counting, such as ʿalīm. For the pure Arab who remains upon his natural disposition did not understand from ḥakīm other than that it is converted from fāʿil for exaggeration. Do you not see that when he heard a reciter reciting: 'And the thief, male and female, cut off their hands, as a recompense for what they earned, an exemplary punishment from Allah, and Allah is Forgiving, Merciful', he objected that this should be the closing of the preceding construction, 'and Allah is Forgiving, Merciful'? It was said to him: the recitation is 'and Allah is Mighty, Wise', and he said: 'So it should be: He was mighty, so He judged and so He cut.' So he understood from ḥakīm that it is converted for the aforementioned exaggeration from ḥākim. And the understanding of this Arab is a decisive proof for what we have said; and this is an easy and entirely acceptable analysis, which removes those affectations and tangled constructions from which the Book of Allah is to be held exempt."

"As for the reading of Ibn ʿAbbās, we say the same, and we do not make «أنَّ الدين» governed by «شهد» as they claimed, and that «إنه لا إله إلا هو» is parenthetical, meaning between the ḥāl and its owner and between «شهد» and its object (and its clarification will come); rather we say: the object of «شهد» is «إنه» with kasra, according to the analysis of one who analyzed that «شهد», being in the sense of speech, causes what follows it to take kasra, treating it as speech; or we say «إنه» is its object and was suspended (taʿlīq), and the lām did not enter the khabar because it is negated, unlike if it were affirmative, for you say 'I testified that Zayd is indeed departing', so it is suspended with inna together with the presence of the lām, since if there were no lām you would put fatḥa on «أنَّ» and say 'I testified that Zayd is departing'. So whoever reads «أنه» with fatḥa did not intend suspension; and whoever puts kasra intended suspension, and the lām did not enter the khabar because it is negated, as we mentioned." End of quotation.

When the Shaykh mentioned the separation and the parenthetical clauses between the words of this verse, he said, verbatim: "As for the reading of Ibn ʿAbbās, it was analyzed so that {أنَّ الدِّينَ عِندَ الله الإسلام} is the object of «شهد», and there are two parentheticals in the speech: one between the conjoined-to and the conjoined, namely «إنه لا إله إلا هو»; the second between the conjoined and the ḥāl and the object of «شَهِدَ», namely «لا إله إلا هو العزيز الحكيم»; and if we parse «العزيز الحكيم» as the khabar of an omitted mubtadaʾ, that makes three parentheticals. Look at these remote directions, whose like no one can bring from the speech of the Arabs; what led to that was only non-Arab origin (ʿujma) and the lack of deep study of the constructions of the Arabs' speech and memorization of their poetry; and as we pointed out in the preface of this book, grammar alone will not suffice for knowledge of the eloquent among the speech of the Arabs; rather it is necessary to be acquainted with the speech of the Arabs, to take on their natures, and to do much of that."

I (al-Samīn) say: his attributing the speech of the luminaries of the Umma to non-Arab origin and their lack of knowledge of the speech of the Arabs, and their placing the speech of Allah upon what is not permissible, and that this view he mentioned is an easy, clear analysis, is not accepted nor conceded; rather what comes first to the mind is what the people transmitted, and those parentheticals within the words of the noble verse have their like in the speech of the Arabs. How could al-Fārisī, al-Zamakhsharī, al-Farrāʾ and their like be ignorant of that, and how can he boast of acquaintance with what the like of these were not acquainted with? And how can it be thought of al-Zamakhsharī that he does not know the places of composition (naẓm), when he is the one conceded to in the sciences of meanings, bayān and badīʿ? No one doubts that whoever engages with the science of exegesis must know a good portion of these sciences. Look at what the author of al-Kashshāf related in his preface from al-Jāḥiẓ, and what he mentioned about one ignorant of these sciences. But the Shaykh denies that and claims that these sciences are not needed at all; hence what I mentioned from him arose.

His saying: {عِندَ الله}: an adverb, the governor in it being the word «الدين», because of the verbal meaning it includes. Abū l-Baqāʾ said: "it cannot be a ḥāl, because inna does not govern a ḥāl." I say: they have allowed «layta», «ka-anna» and «hā» to govern a ḥāl. They said: because of what these particles include of the meaning of wishing, comparison and alerting; and since inna is for emphasis, let it too govern a ḥāl; it is not far from the «hā» of alerting, rather it is more fitting than it, for it is a governing particle while «hā» is not, so it is nearer to the resemblance of a verb than «hā».

His saying: {بَغْياً}: it has several views. The first: that it is mafʿūl li-ajlihi (object of purpose), the governor in it being «اختلف», and the exception is "emptied" (mufarragh). The implied form is: "They differed only out of envy, not for anything else." The second: that it is a maṣdar in the position of accusative as ḥāl from «الذين», as if it were said: "they differed only in this state"; it is not strong, and the exception is also emptied. [The third: that it is accusative as a maṣdar and its governor is implied,] as if when it was said "they did not differ", it indicated the meaning "and they did not transgress", so it is a maṣdar of emphasis; this is the view of al-Zajjāj, and the first is the view of al-Akhfash, which Abū ʿAlī preferred. Two excepted items occurred after «إلا», namely «مِنْ بعدِ» and «بَغْياً»; the analysis of that has preceded, and what the people mentioned on it.

His saying: {وَمَن يَكْفُرْ}: «مَنْ» is a mubtadaʾ, and in its khabar are the three views, I mean the protasis alone, or the apodosis alone, or both. On the view that it is the apodosis alone, a latent pronoun is necessary, that is: "swift in reckoning for him"; the verification of that has preceded.

semin-durr:96-96.t:
His saying, the Exalted: {وُضِعَ لِلنَّاسِ}: this clause is in the position of genitive as an adjective of «بيت». The majority read «وُضِع» in the passive; ʿIkrima and Ibn al-Samayfaʿ read «وَضَع» in the active, and about its agent there are two views, the more apparent being that it is the pronoun of Ibrāhīm, because he was mentioned earlier and because he is famed for building it; the second is that it is the pronoun of the Creator, the Exalted. And «للناس» is attached to the verb before it, the lām in it being for cause (ʿilla). And «لَلَّذي بِبَكَّةَ» is the khabar (predicate) of إنّ. It informed here with a definite, which is the relative, about an indefinite, which is «أولَ بيت», because the indefinite was specified by two things: the annexation and the description by the clause after it; and this is permissible in the chapter of إنّ. Among Sībawayh's expressions is: «إنَّ قريباً منك زيدٌ»; when «قريباً» was specified by its description with the preposition-and-noun phrase after it, what I mentioned to you became allowable. What adds to its goodness here is that it is the ism (noun) of «إنّ», and an indefinite has occurred as the ism of إنّ even without specification. The poet said:
1357 - وإنَّ حَراماً أَنْ أَسُبَّ مجاشعاً ... بآبائيَ الشُمِّ الكرامِ الخَضَارمِ
(Indeed it is forbidden that I revile Mujāshiʿ by my fathers, the lofty, noble, abundantly generous.)
And «ببكة» is a ṣila (relative clause), and the bāʾ in it is locative, that is: in Makka. About بَكَّة there are several views. One: that it is a synonym of مكة, its mīm having been replaced by bāʾ. They said: the Arabs alternate between the bāʾ and the mīm in places; they said: "هذا عليَّ ضَرْبَةُ لازم ولازِب", "وهذا أمرٌ راتِب وراتِم", النَّمِيط and النَّبيط, "سَبَدَ رأسه وسَمَدَها", and "أَعْبطت الحُمَّى وأَعْمَطَت". It was said: it is the name of the inner part of Makka; it was said: of the place of the House; it was said: of the mosque itself, and they supported this by the fact that التباكّ, which is crowding, occurs only at the circumambulation; one says: تَبَاكَّ الناسُ, that is, they crowded. This view is invalidated, some said, by a thing's being a location for itself, and it is invalid, because the House is truly in the mosque, and it was named بكة for the crowding of the people. It was said: because it breaks (تَبُكُّ) the necks of the tyrants, that is, crushes them. And مكة was named from their saying «تَمَكَّكْتُ المُخَّ من العظم», when you extracted it fully and left nothing of it; from which: «امْتَكَّ الفصيلُ ما في ضَرْع أمه» when it leaves no milk in it. It is reported that he said: «لا تُمَكِّكُوا على غرمائِكم» (Do not exhaust your debtors).
Then in its being so named there are several views. Ibn al-Anbārī said: "It was so named because of the scarcity of its water, crops and fertility, so it is taken from «مَكَكْتُ العظمَ» when you leave nothing in it. It was said: because whoever does wrong in it, Allah exhausts him (مَكَّه), that is, utterly destroys him. It was said: because it is the middle of the earth like the marrow in the middle of the bone, and this is the view of al-Khalīl ibn Aḥmad, and it is good." The مَكُّوك is a cup that is drunk from and measured with, like the ṣuwāʿ.
His saying: {مُبَارَكاً وَهُدًى}: two ḥāls (circumstantials): either from the pronoun in «وُضِع», as Abū l-Baqāʾ and others gave its i'rab, but there is some doubt in it, in that it requires separation between the ḥāl and its operator by an outsider, which is the khabar of إنّ, and that is not permissible, because the khabar is governed by إنّ. But if you imply an operator, namely «وُضِع», after «للذي ببكة», that is, "and it was placed", it is allowable; and what impelled to that is what the exegesis of the Commander of the Believers gives, that it was placed with this qualification.
The apparent is that «وهدى» is conjoined to «مباركاً». Some claimed that it is the khabar of an implied mubtadaʾ, its implied form being "and it is guidance", but that is of no account.
البركة is increase; one says: باركَ الله لك, that is, He increased good for you; it is transitive, and {أَن بُورِكَ مَن} [النمل: 8] indicates this, and it is made to include the meaning of [what is transitivized] by «على», as in His saying: {وَبَارَكْنَا عَلَيْهِ} [الصافات: 113]. And «تبارَكَ» is not conjugated and is not used as a predicate except of Allah the Exalted, and its meaning with respect to Him, the Exalted, is that His goodness and beneficence increased. It was said: البَرَكَةُ is the permanence of good, taken from مَبْرَك البعير (the camel's kneeling place). Or [the ḥāl is] from the latent pronoun in the preposition-and-noun phrase, which is «ببكة», because it occurs as a ṣila, the operator in it being the preposition-and-noun phrase by what it contains of settledness, or the operator in the preposition. It is also permissible that it be accusative by the implication of a verb of praise, or as ikhtiṣāṣ (specification); and its being indefinite does no harm, and the evidences of that have preceded. And «للعالمين» is like His saying: {لِّلْمُتَّقِينَ} [الآية: 2] at the beginning of al-Baqara.

semin-durr:110-110.t:
His saying, the Exalted: {كُنْتُمْ خَيْرَ أُمَّةٍ}: concerning this «كان» there are six views. First: that it is the incomplete verb (nāqiṣa) on its usual footing. If so, it does not indicate pastness and cessation; rather it can be used for cessation, as in «كان زيد قائماً», and for permanence, as in {وَكَانَ الله غَفُوراً رَّحِيماً} [al-Nisāʾ: 16] and {وَلاَ تَقْرَبُواْ الزنى إِنَّهُ كَانَ فَاحِشَةً} [al-Isrāʾ: 32]. Here it is equivalent to «لم يَزَلْ» (has never ceased), and this is according to the contextual indications.

al-Zamakhsharī said: «كان» is an expression for the existence of a thing in a past time, in an indefinite manner, and it contains no indication of a prior non-existence nor of a subsequent cessation. Of this is His saying, the Exalted: {وَكَانَ الله غَفُوراً رَّحِيماً}, and His saying {كُنْتُمْ خَيْرَ أُمَّةٍ}, as if it were said «وُجِدْتُم خيرَ أمة» ("you were found the best community"). The Shaykh [Abū Ḥayyān] said: His saying "it does not indicate prior non-existence" holds when it does not mean «صار» (became); when it means «صار» it does indicate prior non-existence. If you say «كان زيد عالماً» in the sense of «صار زيد عالماً», it indicates that he moved from the state of ignorance to the state of knowledge. As for his saying "nor a subsequent cessation", we mentioned before that the sound view is that it is like the other verbs: the past wording of it indicates cessation, and then it may be used where there is no cessation, and there is a difference between indication and usage. Do you not see that you say "this word indicates generality", and then it may be used where generality is not meant but rather specificity? And his saying "as if it were said: you were found the best community" conflicts with his saying that it is like {وَكَانَ الله غَفُوراً رَّحِيماً}, because his implied form "you were found the best community" indicates that it is the complete verb and that «خير أمة» is a ḥāl, whereas in {وَكَانَ الله غَفُوراً رَّحِيماً} it is without doubt the incomplete verb; so the two conflict. I say: there is no conflict, because this is an explanation of meaning, not an explanation of i'rab.

Second: that it means «صِرْتُم» (you became); and «كان» often comes in the sense of «صار», as in his saying:
1385 - بتيهاءَ قَفْرٍ والمَطِيُّ كأنها ... قَطَا الحَزْنِ قد كانَتْ فِراخا بيوضُها
(In a barren trackless desert, the riding camels like sandgrouse of the rough ground, whose eggs have become chicks.)
that is: they became chicks.
Third: that it is complete, meaning «وُجِدْتُم» (you were found), and «خيرَ أمة» on this basis is accusative as a ḥāl, i.e. "you were found in this state".
Fourth: that it is redundant (zāʾida), the implied form being "you are the best community". This is a weak view, or a mistake, for two reasons. One: it is not added at the beginning, and Ibn Mālik transmitted agreement on that. The second: it does not govern «خير» while redundant; and in the second there is room for objection, since redundancy does not negate governing, and evidence for this was given earlier in al-Baqara at His saying {أَلاَّ نُقَاتِلَ فِي سَبِيلِ الله} [al-Baqara: 246].
Fifth: that it is on its usual footing, and what is meant is "you were, in Allah's knowledge", or "in the Preserved Tablet".
Sixth: that this sentence is connected to His saying {فَفِي رَحْمَةِ الله}, i.e. it will be said to them on the Day of Resurrection {كُنْتُمْ خَيْرَ أُمَّةٍ}; and this is very remote.

His saying: {أُخْرِجَتْ}: this sentence may be in the position of genitive as an adjective of «أمة», which is the apparent view, or in the position of accusative as an adjective of «خير». In that case the wording of the overt noun is observed after it occurs following the second-person pronoun; and had the second-person pronoun been observed, that too would be permissible. That is: when a present pronoun (speaker or addressee) comes first, then its predicate comes as an overt noun, and after that overt noun comes something that can serve as a description of it, the Arabs have two ways. One: observing that preceding pronoun, so that the sentence serving as description of the overt noun / agrees with it; the other: observing that overt noun, so that the pronoun returning to it from the sentence is in the third person. For example, your saying «أنتَ رجلٌ تأمرُ بمعروفٍ» with address observing «أنت», and «يأمر» in the third person observing «رجل»; «وأنا امرؤ أقولُ الحق» in the first person observing «أنا», and «يقولُ الحقَّ» observing «امرؤ». Of observing the pronoun is His saying, the Exalted: {بَلْ أَنتُمْ قَوْمٌ تَجْهَلُونَ} [al-Naml: 55], {بَلْ أَنتُمْ قَوْمٌ تُفْتَنُونَ} [al-Naml: 47], and his saying «وإنك امرؤٌ فيك جاهلية» ("You are a man in whom there is jāhiliyya"), and the poet's saying:
1386 - وأنت امرؤٌ قد كَثَّأَتْ لك لِحْيَةٌ ... كأنك منها قاعدٌ في جُوالِقِ
(You are a man whose beard has grown thick, as if you were sitting in a sack because of it.)
Had it been said in the noble verse «أُخْرِجْتُم», observing «كنتم», it would have been permissible in wording, but it cannot be recited so, because recitation is a followed sunna. It is therefore preferable to make the sentence an adjective of «أمة», not of «خير», so that the address in «تأمرون» is in harmony.

His saying «للناسِ»: there are several aspects. One: that it is attached to «أُخْرجت». Second: that it is attached to «خير»; the difference between them in meaning is that on the second aspect it does not follow that they are the best of communities in all respects, but only in this respect. Third: that it is attached, in meaning but not in i'rab, to «تأمرون», its genitive being a direct object; when it was put first, the governing verb weakened and was strengthened by the added lām, as in {إِن كُنتُمْ لِلرُّؤْيَا تَعْبُرُونَ} [Yūsuf: 43], i.e. "you interpret the dream".

His saying «تأمرون»: in this sentence there are several aspects. One: that it is a second khabar of «كنتم», observing the earlier pronoun in «كنتم»; had it observed the khabar it would have said «يأمرون» in the third person, and this was verified earlier. Second: that it is in the position of accusative as a ḥāl; said by al-Rāghib and Ibn ʿAṭiyya. Third: that it is in the position of accusative as an adjective of «خير أمة», and address was used for the reason given; said by al-Ḥawfī. Fourth: that it is resumptive, explaining by it their being the best community, as if it were said: the cause of your being the best of communities is these praiseworthy qualities; and this is the strangest of the aspects.

His saying: {لَكَانَ خَيْراً}: the subject of «كان» is a pronoun returning to the verbal noun indicated by its verb; the implied form being "belief would have been better", as they say «مَنْ كَذَبَ كان شراً له», i.e. lying would have been evil for him; and like it {اعدلوا هُوَ أَقْرَبُ} [al-Māʾida: 8], [and his saying]:
1387 - إذا نُهِي السَّفيهُ جَرَى إليه ... وخالفَ والسَّفِيهُ إلى خلافِ
(When the fool is forbidden, he runs toward it and defies; and the fool runs to opposition.)
that is: folly ran toward it.
That which is surpassed (al-mufaḍḍal ʿalayhi) is omitted, i.e. "better for them than their disbelief and their persisting in their ignorance". [Translator's note: the source then has an incomplete sentence: "And what is meant by betterness in their claim:" with nothing following.] Ibn ʿAṭiyya said: "The word «خير» is a comparative form, and there is no sharing of goodness between their disbelief and their belief; it is permissible only because of the wide extension and many branches of the word «خير», and likewise are the words «أفضل» and «أحب» and what follows their course." The Shaykh said: "Keeping it on its original sense is preferable when that is possible, and it is possible here, since betterness is unrestricted, and so it is obtained by the least sharing."

His saying: {مِّنْهُمُ المؤمنون} to its end: He made it resumptive, brought to report that.

semin-durr:111-111.t:
His saying, the Exalted: {إِلاَّ أَذًى}: there are two aspects. One: that it is a connected exception (muttaṣil), an unrestricted exception (mufarragh) from the general maṣdar, as if it were said: "They will never harm you any harm at all, except a harm of annoyance which is of no concern, from an evil word and the like." The second: that it is a disconnected exception (munqaṭiʿ), i.e. "they will never harm you by fighting and overcoming, but by a word of annoyance and the like."

His saying: {ثُمَّ لاَ يُنصَرُونَ} is resumptive, and it is not jussive by conjoining to the apodosis, because the meaning would change: Allah the Exalted reported their lack of help absolutely, and had we conjoined it to the apodosis it would have been necessary to restrict it to their fighting us, whereas they are unhelped absolutely, whether they fight or do not fight. Some who lack discernment claimed that what is conjoined to the apodosis by «ثم» can never be jussive. He said: "Because what is conjoined to the apodosis is an apodosis, and the apodosis of a condition occurs after it and immediately following it, while «ثم» implies delay, so how can its occurring immediately after the condition be conceived? Therefore it is not made jussive with «ثم»." This is wholly invalid because of His saying, the Exalted: {وَإِن تَتَوَلَّوْاْ يَسْتَبْدِلْ قَوْماً غَيْرَكُمْ ثُمَّ لاَ يكونوا أَمْثَالَكُم} [Muḥammad: 38], for «لا يكونوا» is jussive as a sequence to «يستبدل», which stands as the apodosis, and the conjunction is «ثم». «الأدبارَ» is the second object of «ليولُّوكم», because it became transitive by doubling (taḍʿīf) to another object.

semin-durr:112-112.t:
His saying, the Exalted: {أَيْنَ مَا ثقفوا}: «أينما» is a conditional; it is an adverb of place, and «ما» is added to it; so «ثُقفوا» is in the position of jussive by it. The apodosis of the condition is either omitted, i.e. "wherever they are found they are overcome and humiliated", indicated by His saying {ضُرِبَتْ عَلَيْهِمُ الذلة}; or it is «ضُرِبَتْ» itself, according to those who permit the apodosis to precede the condition. {ضُرِبَتْ عَلَيْهِمُ الذلة} has no grammatical position on the first view, and its position is jussive on the second.

His saying: {إِلاَّ بِحَبْلٍ}: this prepositional phrase is in the position of accusative as a ḥāl, and it is an unrestricted exception (mufarragh) from the general states. al-Zamakhsharī said: "It is an exception from the most general of the general states, and the meaning is: 'Humiliation is struck upon them in all states except the state of their holding fast to a rope from Allah and a rope from the people.'" On this basis it is a connected exception. al-Zajjāj and al-Farrāʾ said: "It is a disconnected exception." al-Farrāʾ implied: «إلاَّ أَنْ يَعْتصموا بحبل من الله», omitting what the prepositional phrase attaches to, as Ḥumayd ibn Thawr al-Hilālī said:
1388 - رَأَتْني بِحَبْلَيْها فَصَدَّتْ مخافةً ... وفي الحبلِ رَوْعاءُ الفؤادِ فَروقُ
(She saw me with her two ropes and turned away in fear; and in the rope there was a startled, fearful heart.)
He meant: «أقبلت بحبليها» ("she approached with her two ropes"), omitting the verb because of the indication of it. Ibn ʿAṭiyya gave as a parallel His saying, the Exalted: {وَمَا كَانَ لِمُؤْمِنٍ أَن يَقْتُلَ مُؤْمِناً إِلاَّ خَطَأً} [al-Nisāʾ: 92]. He said: "Because the first impression gives that he may kill by mistake, and that the rope from Allah and from the people removes the striking of humiliation; but it is not so. Rather there is an omission in the speech / that the understanding of the listener who considers the matter grasps, and its implied form in our verse is: «فلا نجاة من الموت إلا بحبلٍ» ('there is no escape from death except by a rope')." The Shaykh said: "On what he implied it is not a disconnected exception, because it is an exception from an implied sentence, which is «فلا نجاة من الموت», and it is connected on this implication; so it cannot be disconnected from the first, since one exception cannot be both disconnected and connected. The disconnected exception, as established in the science of grammar, is of two kinds: one to which the governing element can be applied, and one to which it cannot. This verse is of the latter on the supposition of disconnection, as the implied form is: 'but their holding fast to a rope from Allah and a rope from the people saves them from killing, captivity, the enslavement of their offspring, and the extermination of their wealth.' What shows that it is disconnected is the report of this in His saying, the Exalted, in Sūrat al-Baqara: {وَضُرِبَتْ عَلَيْهِمُ الذلة والمسكنة وَبَآءُو بِغَضَبٍ مِّنَ الله} [al-Baqara: 61], where He made no exception there." What follows this verse has been parsed earlier.

semin-durr:113-113.t:
His saying, the Exalted: {لَيْسُواْ سَوَآءً}: the apparent view in this verse is that stopping at «سواء» is complete, for the wāw is the subject (ism) of «ليس» and «سواءً» is the predicate, and the wāw refers to the People of the Book mentioned earlier. The meaning is that they are divided into believer and disbeliever, because of His saying {مِّنْهُمُ المؤمنون وَأَكْثَرُهُمُ الفاسقون} [Āl ʿImrān: 110], so their equality is negated. «سواء» is originally a maṣdar (verbal noun), which is why it is in the singular, and its verification was given at the beginning of al-Baqara.

Abū ʿUbayda said: "The wāw in «ليسوا» is a sign of plurality and not a pronoun, and the subject of «ليس» on this view is «أمة», with «قائمة» as its adjective, and likewise «يَتْلُون»." This is according to the dialect of "akalūnī l-barāghīth" ("the fleas ate me"), as in the saying of another:
1389 - يَلُومونني في اشتراءِ النخي ... لِ أَهْلي فكلُّهمُ أَلْوَمُ
(My family blame me for buying the palm trees, and every one of them is more blaming.)
They said: "It is a weak dialect." al-Suhaylī disputed with the grammarians over its being weak, and some attributed it to Azd Shanūʾa; the ḥadīth often comes in it, and there is the like of it in the Qur'an. Its verification will come in al-Māʾida with further explanation.

Ibn ʿAṭiyya said: "What Abū ʿUbayda said is a rejected mistake", and he did not explain the mistake. It is as if he imagined that the subject of «ليس» is only «أمة قائمة», and that nothing is omitted there, since the point is not a difference of the upright community that follows. If something omitted is implied there, Abū ʿUbayda's saying is not a rejected mistake, except that some of them rejected his saying on the ground that it is a weak dialect, and what is in it was mentioned earlier. The implied form by which the meaning is made sound is: "Not equal among the People of the Book are an upright community described as mentioned and a disbelieving community." This is an implication by which the meaning to which Abū ʿUbayda inclined is made sound.

al-Farrāʾ said: "Stopping at «سواء» is not complete." He made the wāw the subject of «ليس» and «سواءً» its predicate, as the majority said, and «أمة» is nominative by «سواء» as a fāʿil, i.e. "the People of the Book are not equal: among them an upright community described as mentioned, and a disbelieving community"; so the balancing sentence was omitted because the first part indicates it, as in the poet's saying:
1390 - دعاني إليها القلبُ إني لأَِمْرِها ... سميعٌ فما أَدْري أَرُشْدٌ طِلابُها
(The heart called me to her; I am obedient to her command, and I do not know whether pursuing her is right guidance.)
that is: «أم غَيٌّ» (or error); so «الغَيّ» was omitted because its opposite indicates it; and like it the saying of another:
1391 - أراكَ فما أَدْرِي أَهَمٌّ هَمَمْتَه ... وذو الهَمِّ قِدْماً خاشِعٌ مُتَضائِلُ
(I see you, and I do not know whether it is a concern you are concerned with; and the man of concern has long been humble and shrunken.)
that is: «أَهَمٌّ هممته أم غيره» (a concern you were concerned with, or something else); it was omitted because of the indication, and this is frequent. al-Farrāʾ said: "Because equality requires two things, as in {سَوَآءً العاكف فِيهِ والباد} [al-Ḥajj: 25] and {سَوَآءً مَّحْيَاهُمْ وَمَمَاتُهُمْ} [al-Jāthiya: 21]." al-Farrāʾ's saying was weakened on the ground of the omission and of putting the overt noun in the place of the pronoun, since the original is "among them an upright community", and «أهلِ الكتابِ» was put in the place of the pronoun.

The better view is that «ليسوا سواءً» is a complete sentence, His saying {مِّنْ أَهْلِ الكتاب أُمَّةٌ} a sentence by itself, and His saying {يَتْلُونَ} another sentence explaining their inequality, just as the sentence beginning {تَأْمُرُونَ بالمعروف} [Āl ʿImrān: 110] etc. explains the superiority. It is also possible that «يتلون» is in the position of nominative as an adjective of «أمة». It may also be a ḥāl from «أمة» because it has been specified by the adjective, or a ḥāl from the pronoun in «قائمة»; and on its being a ḥāl from «أمة» the governing element is the "being established" implied by the prepositional phrase; and it may be a ḥāl from the latent pronoun in this prepositional phrase, because it stands as khabar of «أمة».

His saying: {آنَآءَ الليل} is an adverbial of «يتلون». al-Anāʾ means the hours; its singular is «أنَى» (with fatḥa on hamza and nūn, like «عصا»), or «إنَى» (with kasra on the hamza and fatḥa on the nūn, like «مِعَى»), or «أَنْيٌ» (with fatḥa and sukūn, like «ظَبْي»), or «إنْيٌ» (with kasra and sukūn, like «نِحْي»), or «إنْوٌ» (with kasra and sukūn with wāw, like «جِرْو»). The hamza in «آناء» is converted from yāʾ on the first four views, like ridāʾ, and from wāw on the last view, like kisāʾ. The rest of this root will come in other places.

It is not permissible that «آناء الليل» be an adverbial of «قائمة». Abū l-Baqāʾ said: "Because «قائمة» has been qualified, it does not govern them after the adjective." This is on the supposition that «يَتْلُون» is an adjective of «قائمة», and there is room for objection, because the meaning is not that this sentence be an adjective of what precedes, but rather resumptive for the preceding explanation. And on supposing it to be an adjective of what precedes, it is an adjective of «أمة», not of «قائمة», because an adjective is not itself qualified, unless the meaning of the second adjective suits what precedes it, as in «مرَرْتُ برجلٍ ناطقٍ فصيحٍ», where «فصيح» is an adjective of «ناطق», because its meaning suits it. Some make it an adjective of «رجل». What prevents this adverbial from attaching to «قائمة» is what I mentioned about the resumptive nature of its sentence.

His saying: {وَهُمْ يَسْجُدُونَ}: it may be a ḥāl from the fāʿil of «يَتْلُون», i.e. "they recite the Qur'an while prostrating"; this could be because in their law reciting while prostrating is legitimate, unlike our law, and by this the view of those who say they are not the community of Muḥammad is given preference. It may be / a ḥāl from the pronoun in «قائمة», said by Abū l-Baqāʾ; but it is weak because of the resumption mentioned; and it may be resumptive.

semin-durr:114-114.t: His saying, the Exalted: {يُؤْمِنُونَ} … to its end: it is either resumptive or ḥāls (circumstantial clauses). The first sentence was brought as a nominal sentence to indicate permanence, and was opened with a pronoun, and a verbal sentence was built upon it so that the pronoun is repeated and the speech gains emphasis by its repetition. The khabar was brought in the imperfect to indicate the renewal of prostration at every time, and likewise the sentences after it were brought as imperfect verbs. It is possible that «يؤمنون» is a second khabar of «هم», and for that reason the conjunction is left out; had it been mentioned, that too would have been permissible. His saying {مِنَ الصالحين}: «مِنْ» may be partitive, which is the apparent view. Ibn ʿAṭiyya made it explicative of the kind (bayān al-jins), but there is room for objection in it, since no vague term preceded for this to explain.

semin-durr:115-115.t:
His saying, the Exalted: {وَمَا يَفْعَلُواْ}: the two Kisāʾīs [Ḥamza and al-Kisāʾī] and Ḥafṣ read «يفعلوا» and «يُكْفَروه» in the third person, and the others in the second person. The third person observes His saying {مِّنْ أَهْلِ الكتاب أُمَّةٌ قَآئِمَةٌ}, so it follows the wording of the third person: the Exalted informs us that whatever good they do remains for them, not denied. The second person returns to the address of the community of Muḥammad ﷺ in His saying «كنتم». It is possible that it is an iltifāt (shift) from the third person in His saying {أُمَّةٌ قَآئِمَةٌ} etc. to addressing them, in that He put them at ease with this address; and what supports this is that He limited himself to mentioning good without evil, to increase the putting at ease. The reading of the two Kisāʾīs indicates it, for it is like an explicit text that what is meant is His saying {أُمَّةٌ قَآئِمَةٌ}.

«كَفَر» takes one object, so how does it take two here, the first of which stands in place of the fāʿil (agent) and the second of which is the hāʾ in «يُكْفروه»? It is said: it has been made to include the meaning of a verb taking two objects, namely «حَرَم» (to deprive), as if it were said: «فَلَنْ تُحْرَمُوه» ("you will not be deprived of it"), and «حَرَم» takes two objects.

semin-durr:141-141.t:
And his saying, the Exalted: {وَلِيُمَحِّصَ}: conjoined to «لِيَعْلَمَ», and the sentence {والله لاَ يُحِبُّ الظالمين} is a parenthetical sentence between these reasons. Al-tamḥīṣ: purifying from a thing. It is said that al-maḥṣ is like al-faḥṣ (examination), but al-faḥṣ is said of bringing something out from amid what it is mixed with while it is separate, whereas al-maḥṣ is said of bringing it out from what is attached to it. One says maḥaṣtu al-dhahab and maḥḥaṣtuhu, when you removed from it the dross that mixes with it. Maḥaṣa al-thawb: when he removed its nap (zi'bar). Maḥaṣa al-ḥabl, i.e. it wore out until its nap went from it. Maḥaṣa al-ẓaby: it ran. So maḥaṣa, lightened, can be intransitive and transitive. Thus al-Zajjāj related this word: "al-ḥabl" (the rope); and al-Naqqāsh related it: "maḥaṣa al-jamal" (the camel), when its hair went and it became smooth; both meanings are clear.

Al-Khalīl said: "Al-tamḥīṣ is purifying from a flawed thing. It is also said: it is testing and trial," and he recited:

1443 - رأيْتُ فُضَيْلاً كان شيئاً مُلَفَّفَاً ... فكشَّفَه التمحيصُ حتى بداليا
(I saw Fuḍayl, who had been something wrapped up; the testing uncovered him until he appeared to me.)

Al-Wāḥidī related from al-Mubarrad with a connected chain: maḥaṣa al-ḥablu yamḥaṣu maḥṣan when its nap went until it became smooth; and ḥablun maḥīṣ and malīṣ are of one meaning. He said: "It is desirable in a horse that its legs be maḥaṣ, i.e. clean (taklūṣ)", and Ibn al-Anbārī recited in this regard, describing a mare:

1444 - صُمِّ النُّسورِ صِحاحٍ غيرِ عاثِرَةٍ ... رُكِّبْنَ في مَحِصاتٍ مُلْتَقَى العَصَبِ
(Hard in the hoof-frogs, sound, not stumbling; set upon lean legs, the meeting of the sinews.)

i.e. on legs stripped of flesh in which there is only bone, sinew and skin. Al-Mubarrad said: "The meaning of people's saying «مَحِّصْ عَنَّا ذنوبنا» is: remove what clings to us of sins." Al-Wāḥidī said: "What al-Mubarrad said is the interpretation of al-maḥaṣ with fatḥa on the ḥāʾ, and it is attested, while al-maḥṣ with sukūn on the ḥāʾ is fabricated. Al-Khalīl said: 'One says maḥaṣtu al-shayʾa amḥaṣuhu maḥaṣan when you cleansed it from every flaw.'" In his making the sukūn on the ḥāʾ "fabricated" there is something to consider, because the people of the language transmitted it with sukūn, and it is the analogical maṣdar of the triliteral. Maḥaṣtu al-sayf wa-l-sinān: I polished them until their rust went. Usāma al-Hudhalī said:

1445 - وشَقُّوا بمَمْحوص السِّنانِ فؤادَه ... . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . .
(And they split his heart with a polished spearhead ...)

i.e. with a polished one; and from it that is metaphorically used in describing a rope with smoothness and sheen. Ruʾba said, describing a horse:

1446 - شديدُ جَلْزِ الصُّلْبِ مَمْحُوصُ السَّوَى
(Strong in the binding of the spine, lean in the back.)

And al-sawāʾ is the back; he shortened it out of necessity. It has been heard: "I did it until my sawā was cut off", i.e. my back. The root «مَحَق» has already been discussed in al-Baqara.

semin-durr:142-142.t:
His saying, the Exalted: {أَمْ حَسِبْتُمْ أَن تَدْخُلُواْ}: There are several views on this «أم», the most evident being that it is discontinuous (munqaṭiʿa), estimated as «بل» plus the interrogative hamza, and its meaning is rebuke (inkār). It is also said that «أم» is in the sense of the hamza alone, and its meaning, as has gone before, is reproach and rebuke. It is also said that this is an interrogative whose meaning is prohibition; Abū Muslim al-Iṣfahānī said it. It is also said that it is continuous (muttaṣila). Ibn Baḥr said: "It is the counterpart of a hamza that is estimated from the meaning of what has gone before, for his saying {إِن يَمْسَسْكُمْ قَرْحٌ} {وَتِلْكَ الأيام نُدَاوِلُهَا} to the end of the story requires that it be followed by: 'Do you know that the obligation requires that, or did you suppose'." And «حَسِبَ» here is in its normal sense of preferring one of two sides. And {أَن تَدْخُلُواْ} stands in place of the two objects according to Sībawayh, and in place of the first, the second being omitted, according to al-Akhfash.

His saying: {وَلَمَّا يَعْلَمِ}: a ḥāl sentence. Al-Zamakhsharī said: «ولَمَّا» is in the sense of «لم», except that it has a kind of expectation, so it indicates the negation of striving in the past and its expectation in the future. You say: "He promised me that he would do such and such, and not yet (wa-lammā)", meaning "and he has not done it, and I expect his doing it." The Shaykh (Abū Ḥayyān) said: "This which he said about «لَمَّا», that it indicates expectation of the action negated by it in the future, I do not know any of the grammarians to have mentioned; rather they mentioned that when you say «لَمَّا يخرج زيد» it indicates the non-occurrence of the going out in the past, its negation being continuous up to the time of the report; but that it indicates its expectation in the future, no. However, I found in the speech of al-Farrāʾ something close to what al-Zamakhsharī said: he said that «لَمَّا» is for presenting existence as a possibility, unlike «لم»." I say: The grammarians distinguished between them only from the aspect that what is negated by «لَمْ» is a verb not accompanied by «قد», while «لَمَّا» is its negation accompanied by it, and it may indicate expectation, so al-Zamakhsharī's statement is sound from this aspect. What I said, that «لم» is the negation of faʿala and «لَمَّا» the negation of qad faʿala, is indicated by the explicit statement of the grammarians, Sībawayh and those after him. The like of this verse has gone before in al-Baqara with a verification of the discussion that makes its repetition unnecessary, so turn to it.

And his saying «منكم» is a ḥāl from «الذين». And {وَلَمَّا يَعْلَمِ الله} with kasra on the mīm is on the basis of the meeting of two quiescents. Al-Nakhaʿī and Ibn Wathāb read it with fatḥa on it, and there are two views on this. One: that the fatḥa is a fatḥa of assimilation, the mīm being made to follow the lām before it. The second: that it is based on the intended light nūn (nūn khafīfa), the origin being «ولَمَّا يَعْلَمَنْ»; and what is negated by «لَمَّا» has come emphasized with it, as in his saying:

1447 - يَحْسَبُه الجاهلُ ما لم يَعْلما ... شيخاً على كُرْسِيِّه مُعَمَّماً
(The ignorant, as long as he does not know, takes him to be a sheikh on his chair, turbaned.)

When he dropped the nūn the end of the verb remained with fatḥa, as in his saying:

1448 - لا تُهِينَ الفقيرَ عَلَّك أَنْ تَرْ ... كَعَ يوماً والدهرُ قد رَفَعَهْ
(Do not humiliate the poor man; perhaps you will one day bow down while time has raised him.)

[and on this is analysed the reading «ألم نشرحَ» with fatḥa on the ḥāʾ], and the saying of another:

1449 - في أيِّ يَوميَّ من الموتِ أفِرْ ... أيومَ لم يُقْدَرَ أم يومَ قُدِرْ
(On which of my two days shall I flee from death: the day not decreed, or the day decreed?)

His saying: «ويَعْلَم»: the majority read with fatḥa on the mīm, and there are two analyses of it. The more famous: that the verb is accusative. Then is its being accusative by an implied «أَنْ» after the wāw that signifies concurrence (jamʿ), as in your saying «لا تأكلِ السمكَ وتَشْربَ اللبن» (do not eat fish and drink milk), i.e. do not combine the two, which is the view of the Basrans; or by the wāw of diversion (wāw al-ṣarf), which is the view of the Kufans, meaning that it was proper for this verb to take the same case ending as what precedes it, but when the wāw came it diverted it to another aspect of i'rab. The exposition of the two schools is elsewhere than this topic.

The second: that the fatḥa is the fatḥa of [two quiescents' meeting, the verb being jussive]; when another quiescent followed it, its end needed a vowel, and the fatḥa was preferable because it is lighter and by assimilation to the vowel of the lām, as was said in one of the two analyses of the reading {وَلَمَّا يَعْلَمِ الله} with fatḥa on the mīm; the first is the better view. [Translator's note: the source text here reads "فتحة التاء ساكنين" and is evidently corrupt; the bracketed rendering is an interpretive reconstruction.]

Al-Ḥasan, Ibn Yaʿmar and Abū Ḥaywa read with kasra on the mīm, conjoining to «يَعْلَمِ» which is jussive by «لم».

ʿAbd al-Wārith read from Abū ʿAmr ibn al-ʿAlāʾ: «وَيَعْلَمُ» in the nominative, with two views. The more evident: that it is a resumption, Allah the Exalted informing of that. Al-Zamakhsharī said: "on the basis that the wāw is circumstantial, as if he said: 'when they have not yet striven while you are steadfast'." The Shaykh said: "What he said is not sound, because the wāw of ḥāl does not enter upon the imperfect; it is not permissible to say «جاء زَيدٌ ويضحك» meaning 'Zayd came laughing', because the imperfect takes the place of the active participle, so just as «جاء زيد وضاحكاً» is not permissible, so «جاء زيد ويضحك» is not permissible. If it is interpreted as the imperfect being the khabar of an omitted mubtadaʾ, that estimate is possible, i.e. «وهو يعلمُ الصابرين» ('and He knows the steadfast'), as they interpreted the poet's saying:

1450 -. . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . ... نَجَوْتُ وَأَرْهُنُهمْ مالِكا
(... I escaped, and I [was] pledging Mālik to them.)

i.e. «وأنا أَرْهُنُهم»." I say: His saying "does not enter upon the imperfect" is not absolute; rather he ought to have said: upon the affirmative imperfect or that negated by «لا», for it enters upon the imperfect negated by «لم» and «لما», as has been known more than once.

semin-durr:143-143.t:
His saying, the Exalted: {كُنْتُمْ تَمَنَّوْنَ}: Al-Bazzī, with a variation from him, read «تَّمَنَّوْنَ» with doubling of the تاء, and that is possible only in waṣl; his rule is that he joins the plural mīm with a wāw, and the verification of this has already been given at his saying {وَلاَ تَيَمَّمُواْ الخبيث} [al-Baqara: 267].

The pronoun in «تَلْقَوه» has two views. The more evident: that it refers back to death; the second: that it refers back to the enemy, although it has not been mentioned, because the situation indicates it.

The majority read «قبل» with kasra on the lām, because it is declinable (muʿrab) owing to its being annexed to «أَنْ» and what is in its scope, i.e. "before meeting it". Mujāhid ibn Jabr read «من قبلُ» with ḍamma on the lām, cut off from annexation, as in his saying {لِلَّهِ الأمر مِن قَبْلُ وَمِن بَعْدُ} [al-Rūm: 4]. On this, «أَنْ» and what is in its scope is in the position of the accusative as a badal ishtimāl (inclusive substitute) from «الموت», i.e. "you wished for the meeting with death", like your saying «رَهَبْتُ العدوَّ لقاءَه» ("I feared the enemy, meeting him"). Al-Zuhrī and al-Nakhaʿī read «تُلاقُوه», and its meaning is the meaning of «تَلْقَوه», because laqiya customarily calls for being between two, even if it is not on the pattern mufāʿala.

His saying: {فَقَدْ رَأَيْتُمُوهُ}: the apparent view is that the seeing is visual, so it suffices with one object. They allowed that it be mental (ʿilmiyya), in which case it needs a second object, which is omitted, i.e. "you have known it present", meaning death; except that omitting one of the two objects in the chapter of ẓanna is not easy, so that some restrict it to poetic necessity, such as the saying of ʿAntara:

1451 - وَلَقَدْ نَزَلْتِ فلا تَظُنِّي غيرَه ... مِنِّي بمنزلةِ المُحَبِّ المُكْرَمِ
(You have alighted [in my heart], so do not suppose otherwise from me, in the station of the honoured beloved.)

i.e. "so do not suppose anything else to be coming from me."

His saying: {وَأَنْتُمْ تَنظُرُونَ}: it may be circumstantial, and then it is a confirming ḥāl (ḥāl muʾakkida) that removes what seeing admits of figurative use or homonymy, i.e. between it and seeing with the heart; or it may be a resumption, meaning: "and you are looking into your conduct now after the war has ended, whether you fulfilled or went against it". Ibn al-Anbārī said: "«رأيتموه» means you faced it while you were looking with your eyes, and for this reason He mentioned looking after seeing when their meanings differed, because the first is in the sense of facing and confronting, and the second in the sense of seeing with the eye." This is not known among the people of the language, I mean the use of seeing for facing and confronting; and on the assumption that it is sound, the sentence {وَأَنْتُمْ تَنظُرُونَ} would be a clarifying ḥāl sentence, not a confirming one, because it conveys a meaning additional to the meaning of its governor. An object may be estimated for «ينظرون», and it may not be estimated, since the meaning is: "and you are people of looking." And Allah the Exalted knows best, and to Allah belong praise and favour.

semin-durr:164-164.t:
His saying, the Exalted: {لَقَدْ مَنَّ الله}: The response of an omitted oath.
It was also read «لِمنْ مَنِّ الله» with the preposition «مِنْ», and «مَنِّ» with shadda is genitive by it. Al-Zamakhsharī analysed it in two ways. One: that this preposition and its genitive noun is a fronted khabar and the mubtadaʾ is omitted, its implied form being: "Of the favour of Allah upon the believers is His favour, or His sending (of a messenger), when He sent"; it was omitted because the indication is present. The second: that the mubtadaʾ is made «إذ» itself, in the sense of "time", and its khabar is the preposition phrase before it, the implied form being: "Of Allah's favour upon the believers is the time of His sending (him)"; and he compared it to their saying: "The most eloquent the emir is when he is standing" (akhṭabu mā yakūnu l-amīru idhā kāna qāʾiman). These two aspects in this reading are among the things that indicate how firmly planted his foot is in this science.
The Shaykh (Abū Ḥayyān), however, rejected the second aspect from him, because «إذ» is non-declinable (ghayr mutaṣarrifa); it is only an adverb, or has a time noun annexed to it, or is an object of "remember" according to one view. He transmitted the statement of Abū ʿAlī about it and «إذا», that the two are not agents, nor objects, nor mubtadaʾs. He said: "It is not preserved from their speech: 'idh qāma Zaydun ṭawīl'", meaning "the time of his standing is long". And (he rejected it) because his comparison of the reading with their saying «أخطبُ» etc. is an error, in that the thing likened is a mubtadaʾ and the thing likened to [it] is an adverb in the position of the khabar according to the one who gives it this i'rab, and in that this khabar, which he has brought out overtly, must be omitted since the ḥāl takes its place, as the grammarians who give it this i'rab have stated explicitly; so how could he bring it out in the wording?" The answer to this rejection is plain, and would that Abū l-Qāsim had not mentioned an analysis of this reading, so that we might have heard...
The majority read «أنفسهم» with ḍamma on the sīn, that is: from among them and of their kind. ʿĀʾisha, Fāṭima and al-Ḍaḥḥāk read it, and Anas related it from him, may Allah bless him and grant him peace, with fatḥa on the fāʾ, from nafāsa, which is nobility, that is: the noblest of them in lineage, creation and character. And from ʿAlī from him, peace be upon him: "I am the noblest of you in lineage, standing and in-law relationship."
This preposition phrase has two possible aspects. One: that it is attached to «بعث» itself. The second: that it is attached to an omitted word as an adjective of «رسولاً», so it would be accusative in position; and this aspect is strengthened on the reading with fatḥa on the fāʾ. His saying {يَتْلُواْ عَلَيْهِمْ} is in the position of a ḥāl or is resumptive, and its parallel has already preceded in al-Baqara.
His saying: {وَإِن كَانُواْ مِن قَبْلُ لَفِي}: This is the lightened «إنْ», and the lām is the distinguishing one (lām fāriqa); discussion on the verification of this and the disagreement about it has already preceded. Only, here al-Zamakhsharī and Makkī, when they made it lightened, implied for it an omitted noun. Al-Zamakhsharī said: "Its implied form is: 'and indeed the matter and the affair — they were before'." Makkī said: "As for Sībawayh, he says it is lightened and its noun is a latent pronoun", the implied form, according to his view, being "and indeed they were". This is not good, because the lightened «إنْ» operates only on an overt noun, on a less eloquent usage, and has no operation on a pronoun, and no omitted noun is implied for it at all; rather, it is neglected (made inoperative) or it operates as has preceded. Moreover, al-Zamakhsharī did not state explicitly that its noun is omitted, but said: "«إنْ» is the lightened one and the lām is the distinguishing one, and the implied form is: 'and indeed the matter and the affair were'", so this may be an explanation of meaning, not of i'rab.
There are two views about this sentence. One: that it is resumptive, with no grammatical position. The second: that it is in the position of an accusative as a ḥāl from the object in «يُعَلِّمُهم», and this is the more evident.

semin-durr:165-165.t:
His saying, the Exalted: {أَوَ لَمَّا أَصَابَتْكُمْ}: The hamza is for denunciation (inkār), and Ibn ʿAṭiyya made it for affirmation (taqrīr). The wāw is a conjunction, and it is intended to be placed before the hamza, as established. Al-Zamakhsharī said: "«لَمَّا» is accusative by «قلتم», and «أصابَتْكم» is in the position of genitive through the annexation of «لَمَّا» to it, and its implied form is 'you said when it struck you'; and «أنَّى هذا» is accusative because it is what is said (maqūl). The hamza is for rebuke and affirmation. If you say: to what does the wāw join this sentence? I say: to what has passed of the story of Uḥud, and His saying {وَلَقَدْ صَدَقَكُمُ الله وَعْدَهُ}; it is also possible that it be conjoined to an omitted sentence, its implied form being: 'Did you do such-and-such, and say at that time such-and-such?'" End of quotation.
As for his making «لَمَّا» have the meaning of «حين», that is an adverb, this is the position of al-Fārisī, and the exposition of the two positions has already preceded. As for his saying "a conjunction upon the story of Uḥud", this is not his position, because what runs from his position is only the implying of a sentence upon which what follows the wāw, or the fāʾ, or «thumma» is conjoined, as he himself laid out in the second aspect.
«أنى هذا»: «أنَّى» has the meaning of «مِن أين» (from where), as has preceded in His saying {أنى لَكِ هذا} [آل عمران: 37]. His saying {مِنْ عِندِ أَنْفُسِكُمْ} and {مِنْ عِندِ الله} indicates this; so said al-Zamakhsharī. The Shaykh rejected this from him, saying that an adverb, when it occurs as a khabar, is not implied as having a preposition other than «في» enter upon it; as for implying «مِنْ» entering upon it, no, because it became accusative only by dropping «في», and for that reason, when the adverb is replaced by a pronoun, [the verb] is made to reach it by «في», unless latitude is used with it. He said: "So his implying it is not valid, and his inference from His saying {مِنْ عِندِ أَنْفُسِكُمْ} {مِنْ عِندِ الله} is a standing on the correspondence of the question to the answer in wording, and a heedlessness of this rule." The Shaykh chose that «أَنَّى» has the meaning of «كيف» (how). He said: "«أنَّى» is a question about the state here, and it does not suit that it mean «أين» or «متى», because the question was not made about a place or time here, but about the state that required that for them. They asked about it by way of wonder, and the answer came in terms of meaning, not wording, in His saying {قُلْ هُوَ مِنْ عِندِ أَنْفُسِكُمْ}." He said: "The question with «أنَّى» is a question about specifying the manner in which this matter came about, and the answer with His saying {مِنْ عِندِ أَنْفُسِكُمْ} implies the specification of the manner, because by specifying the cause the manner is specified in terms of meaning. If it were said by way of wonder: 'How can righteous Zayd not perform the pilgrimage!' and it were said in answer: 'Because of his inability', the answer would be obtained and the meaning would be arranged: he does not perform the pilgrimage since he is unable." End of quotation.
As for his saying "the adverb is not implied with a preposition other than «في»": al-Zamakhsharī did not imply «في» with «أنَّى» so that what he said would follow for him; he only made «أنَّى» equal «من أين» in meaning. As for his departing from the answer that corresponds in wording, the reverse is preferable.
His saying: {قَدْ أَصَبْتُمْ} is in the position of nominative as an adjective of «مصيبة». And «قلتم», on Sībawayh's position, is the response of «لَمَّا», and on al-Fārisī's position it is the accusing operator of it, according to what has preceded of their two positions. The pronoun in His saying «قل» (as in «هو») refers back to the calamity in terms of meaning. It is also possible that it be on the omission of a muḍāf that is taken into account, that is: its cause; and likewise the reference with His saying «أنّى هذا», because what is meant is the calamity.

semin-durr:166-166.t:
His saying, the Exalted: {وَمَآ أَصَابَكُمْ}: «ما» is a relative noun meaning «الذي», in the position of nominative as mubtadaʾ. {فَبِإِذْنِ الله} is the khabar, and it rests on an implied pronoun, its implied form being: "it is by Allah's leave". The fāʾ entered the khabar because of the mubtadaʾ's resemblance to a condition, as in "the one who comes to me — he has a dirham". On what the majority have established this is problematic, because they established that it is not permissible for this fāʾ to enter the khabar as a redundant letter except under conditions, among them that the ṣila be future in meaning; that is because the fāʾ enters only for resemblance to the condition, and the condition is only in the future, not in the past. If you said "the one who came to me yesterday — he has a dirham", it would not be valid. And «أصابَكم» here is past in meaning, because the story is past; so how was the entry of this fāʾ permissible?
They answered that it is understood as clarification (tabyīn), that is: "and whatever is shown to have struck you", just as they interpreted {وَإِنْ كَانَ قَمِيصُهُ قُدَّ مِن دُبُرٍ} [يوسف: 27], that is: if it is shown; and this is an explicit condition. I say: if this interpretation is sound, then let «ما» here be made an explicit conditional, and the fāʾ would be entering obligatorily, as it occurs as the apodosis of the condition. Ibn ʿAṭiyya said: "The entry of the fāʾ is good when [it] is the cause of the giving, and so is the arrangement of this; the meaning is only: 'and what Allah gave leave for is what struck you', but he put first what is most important in their souls and nearest to their perception. Idhn (leave) is enabling something with knowledge of it." This is good in terms of meaning, for the striking is ordered after the leave in meaning. By his saying "the most important and the nearest" he pointed to what struck them on the day the two armies met.
His saying: «وَلِيعٍلَمَ» [Translator's note: the source has a stray diacritic in the printed word]: There are two views about this lām. One: that it is conjoined to the meaning of His saying {فَبِإِذْنِ الله}, the conjunction of a cause upon a cause, so it is attached to what the bāʾ is attached to. The second: that it is attached to an omitted word, that is: "and so that He may know, He did that", that is, it struck you. The first is preferable. It has already preceded that the meaning of "so that Allah may know such-and-such" is distinguishing, and showing to people what was in His knowledge. Some claimed that there is a muḍāf there, that is: "so that He may know the faith of the believers and the hypocrisy of those who…", and there is no need of it.
Translator's note: in the source text of this entry the word «إذا» in "«يَحْسُن دخولُ الفاءِ إذ1اكان سببَ الإِعطاءِ»" is printed with a stray digit ("إذ1اكان"); I have translated it as "when it is" (إذا كان).

semin-durr:167-167.t:
His saying, the Exalted: {وَقِيلَ لَهُمْ تَعَالَوْاْ قَاتِلُواْ}: This sentence has two possible aspects. One: that it is resumptive; Allah informs that they were commanded either to fight or to repel, that is, to swell the ranks of the Muslims. The second: that it is conjoined to «نافقوا», so it falls within the scope of the relative noun, that is: "and so that He may know those from whom hypocrisy and the saying of such-and-such occurred", and «تعالوا» and «قاتِلوا» both stand in the place of the agent for «قيل», because that is what is said, and what is in it has already preceded. Abū l-Baqāʾ said: "He did not bring a conjunction — meaning between «تعالوا» and «قاتِلوا» — because he intended that each of the two sentences be meant in itself; it may also be said that what is meant is the command to fight, and «تعالَوا» mentions something which, had it been left unsaid, there would be in the speech what indicates it; and it was said: the second command is a ḥāl." By his saying "«وتعالوا» mentions something which, had it been left unsaid" he means that what is meant is only their being commanded to fight, not their coming alone; and making «قاتلوا» a ḥāl from «تعالوا» is invalid, because a circumstantial clause must be declarative and this one is a request.
His saying: {أَوِ ادفعوا}: «أو» here is in its usual sense of choice and permission. It was said: it has the meaning of the wāw, because he asked them for fighting and repelling; but the first is the sound view. His saying "they said: if we knew" has no conjunction in this sentence because it is the answer to a questioner's question: as though it were said, "So what did they say when that was said to them?" and the answer was that they said that. And «نعلمُ», though imperfect, has a past meaning, because «لو» restricts the imperfect [to the past] since it is used for what would occur because of the occurrence of something else. He made «قتالاً» indefinite, that is: "if we knew some fighting or other".
His saying: {هُمْ لِلْكُفْرِ يَوْمَئِذٍ أَقْرَبُ}: «هم» is the mubtadaʾ and «أقربُ» its khabar, and it is an elative (afʿal al-tafḍīl); «للكفر» is attached to it, and likewise «للإِيمان». If it is said: "Two prepositions identical in wording and meaning are not attached to one operator, unless one of them is conjoined to the other or is a badal of it; so how were both attached to «أقرب»?" The answer is that this is particular to the elative; they said: because it has the force of two operators, for your saying "Zayd is more excellent than ʿAmr" means that his excellence exceeds the excellence of ʿAmr. Abū l-Baqāʾ said: "It is permissible for «أقربُ» to operate in both, because the two resemble adverbs, just as «أطيبُ» operates in the saying 'this, as unripe dates, is better than it as ripe dates' in the two implied adverbs, since afʿal indicates two meanings: the base of the verb and its excess, so it operates in each of them with a meaning different from the other, and its implied form is: their nearness to disbelief exceeds their nearness to faith."
There is no need to liken the two prepositional phrases to the two adverbs, for the apparent sense is that the justification for their attachment to a single operator is their resemblance to the two adverbs, and it is not so. His saying "the two implied adverbs" means that the meaning is: this at the time of its being unripe is better than it at the time of its being ripe.
«أقربُ» here is from nearness (qurb), which is the opposite of distance, and it is made transitive by three particles: the lām, «إلى» and «مِنْ»; you say qarubtu laka, ilayka and minka. If you say "Zayd is nearer to knowledge than ʿAmr", the first «مِنْ» is the one carrying the base meaning of nearness, and the second is the one governing the one surpassed. Once this is established, there is no need to claim that the lām has the meaning of «إلى».
«يومئذ» is attached to «أقربُ», and so is «منهم»; this «مِنْ» is the one governing the one surpassed after afʿal, and is not the one carrying the base of the verb. The meaning of {هُمْ لِلْكُفْرِ يَوْمَئِذٍ أَقْرَبُ مِنْهُمْ لِلإِيمَانِ} is that before this time they were concealing hypocrisy, so outwardly they were farther from disbelief; then when what they were concealing appeared from them, they became nearer to disbelief.
«إذ» is annexed to an omitted sentence for which the tanwīn is substituted, as its exposition has already preceded, and the implied form of this sentence is: "they were nearer to disbelief on the day when they said: if we knew fighting we would follow you". It was also said: the meaning is on the omission of a muḍāf, that is: "they are nearer to the people of disbelief than to the people of faith". They are here preferred over themselves with respect to two states and two times. Were it not for that, it would not be permissible. You say: "Zayd sitting is better than he standing", or "Zayd sitting today is better than he sitting tomorrow"; and if you said "Zayd today sitting is better than he today sitting" it would not be permissible.
Al-Naqqāsh related from some of the exegetes that «أقرب» here is not from the meaning of nearness which is the opposite of distance, but from qarab with fatḥa on the qāf and rāʾ, which is seeking water, and from it "he sought the water" (qāraba l-māʾ); laylat al-qarab is the night of coming to water. So the meaning is: they are more eager for disbelief; and on this the transitivity by the lām is determined, as in your saying: "Zayd is a harder hitter of ʿAmr".
His saying: {يَقُولُونَ بِأَفْوَاهِهِم}: There are two views about this sentence. One: that it is resumptive, with no position. The second: that it is in the position of accusative as a ḥāl from the pronoun in «أقرب», that is: they drew near to disbelief while saying this statement. His saying «بأفواهِهم» was said to be emphasis, like His saying {وَلاَ طَائِرٍ يَطِيرُ بِجَنَاحَيْهِ} [الأنعام: 38]. The apparent sense is that "saying" applies to both the verbal and the mental, so restricting it with "their mouths" is restricting one of two possibilities, unless it is said that its application to the mental is figurative. Al-Zamakhsharī said: "Mentioning the hearts along with the mouths is a depiction of their hypocrisy, and that their faith exists in their mouths only." By this which al-Zamakhsharī said, its being for emphasis is negated, since it obtains this benefit.

semin-durr:97-97.t:
His saying, the Exalted: {فِيهِ آيَاتٌ}: it is permissible that this clause be in the position of accusative as a ḥāl (circumstantial): either from the pronoun of «وُضع», with the difficulty that has preceded; or from the pronoun in «ببكة», which is clear, and this is according to the opinion of one who permits multiple ḥāls for one owner of a ḥāl; or from the pronoun in «للعالمين»; or from «هدى», and that is allowable because it was specified by the description. It may also be a ḥāl from the pronoun in «مباركاً». It is also permissible that the clause be in the position of accusative as an adjective of «هدى», after its being described by the preposition-and-noun phrase before it. And it is permissible that this clause be resumptive with no grammatical position, brought only as an explanation and clarification of its blessedness and guidance. It is also permissible that the ḥāl or the description, as detailed above, be only the preposition and its genitive noun, with «آياتٌ» nominative by it as an agent (fāʿil), because the preposition-and-noun phrase, whenever it relies on the things I mentioned at the beginning of this topic, raises an agent. This is preferable to making it a clause of mubtadaʾ and khabar, because these things, I mean the ḥāl, the adjective and the khabar, are originally to be single words, so what is closer to them is preferable, and the preposition-and-noun phrase is close to a single word; for that reason the single word is put first, then the adverbial, then the clause, in what I have mentioned. On that is the noble verse: {وَقَالَ رَجُلٌ مُّؤْمِنٌ مِّنْ آلِ فِرْعَوْنَ يَكْتُمُ إِيمَانَهُ} [غافر: 28]; he put first the description by a single word, «مؤمن», second what is close to it, «من آل فرعون», and third the clause, «يكتم إيمانه». The apparent opposite of this has occurred, and I shall make this question clear, if Allah the Exalted wills, at His saying: {يُحِبُّهُمْ وَيُحِبُّونَهُ أَذِلَّةٍ} [المائدة: 54].
His saying: {مَّقَامُ إِبْرَاهِيمَ وَمَن دَخَلَهُ كَانَ آمِناً}: there are several views on it. One: that «مقام» is a badal (substitute) of «آيات». On this it is said that the grammarians stated explicitly that whenever a plural is mentioned, nothing may be substituted for it except what fulfils the plural; so you say: «مررت برجالٍ زيدٍ وعمرٍو وبكر», because the minimum of the sound plural is three. If it does not fulfil it, they said, it is obligatory to cut it off from being a badal: either to the accusative by implying a verb, or to the nominative as a mubtadaʾ whose khabar is omitted; as you say in the preceding example: «زيداً وعمراً», that is, "I mean Zayd and ʿAmr", or «زيد وعمرو», that is, "among them are Zayd and ʿAmr". For that reason they gave the i'rab of the saying of al-Nābigha al-Dhubyānī:
1358 - تَوَهَّمْتُ آياتٍ لها فَعَرَفْتُها ... لستةِ أعوامٍ وذا العامُ سابعُ
رَمادٌ ككحلِ العَيْن لأْياً أُبينه ... ونُؤْيٌ كجِذْم الحَوْضِ أَثْلَمُ خاشعُ
(I made out her signs and recognized them after six years, and this year is the seventh: ashes like eye-kohl that I discern only with difficulty, and a trench like the stump of a trough, notched and humbled.)
according to the cutting-off mentioned above, that is: "among them are ashes and a trench"; and likewise His saying, the Exalted: {حَدِيثُ الجنود فِرْعَوْنَ وَثَمُودَ} [البروج: 17-18], that is: "I mean, or I censure, Pharaoh and Thamūd". Though it may be said that what is meant by Pharaoh and Thamūd is the two together with those of their peoples who followed them, so mentioning them fulfils the plurality. In the noble verse here, after the signs, only two things were mentioned: the Station and the security of whoever enters it; so how can they be a badal? This difficulty also applies to the view of one who made it the khabar of an omitted mubtadaʾ, that is, "they are the Station of Ibrāhīm": how can it inform about a plural with two?
There are replies to it. One: that the minimum of the plural is two, as some held. Al-Zamakhsharī said: "It is also possible that what is meant is: 'In it are signs: the Station of Ibrāhīm and the security of whoever enters it,' because two is a kind of plural like three and four." Second: that «مقام إبراهيم», although single in wording, includes many signs: for the two feet in the solid rock is a sign; their sinking into it up to the ankles is a sign; the softening of part of the rock and not part is a sign; its preservation through the passing of time and its protection from enemies is a sign; and its continuing, unlike the signs of the other prophets, excepting our Prophet, upon him and upon all of them be peace, is a sign. Al-Zamakhsharī said its meaning. Third: that this is of the category of folding (ṭayy), which is that a plural is mentioned, then part of it is brought and silence is kept on mentioning the rest, for a purpose of the speaker, and it is called ṭayy. Al-Zamakhsharī recited for it the saying of Jarīr:
1359 - كانَتْ حُنَيْفَةُ أثلاثاً فثُلْثُهُمُ ... مِنَ العبيدِ وثُلْثٌ مِنْ مَواليها
(Ḥanīfa were in thirds: a third of them slaves, and a third from its freedmen.)
and he brought from it his saying, upon him be peace and blessing: «حُبِّبَ إليَّ من دُنْياكم ثلاثٌ: الطِّيب والنساء، وقُرَّةُ عيني في الصلاة» (Three things of your world were made beloved to me: perfume, women, and the coolness of my eye is in prayer); he mentioned two, which are perfume and women, and folded the mention of the third. It is not said that the third is his saying «وقُرَّةُ عيني في الصلاة», because it is not of their world; it is only of the matters of the hereafter. The benefit of folding, in their view, is the multiplication of that thing, as though when He the Exalted mentioned the sum of the signs by these two signs, He said: "and many besides them". Ibn ʿAṭiyya said: "The more preferable in my view is that the Station and the security of the one who enters were made an example of the signs in the Sanctuary of Allah the Exalted, and were specified in mention because of their greatness, and because the proof is established by them against the disbelievers, since they perceive these two signs with their senses."
The second view: that «مقامُ إبراهيم» is an ʿaṭf bayān (explicative apposition); al-Zamakhsharī said this, and the Shaykh (Abū Ḥayyān) rejected it from the aspect of their differing in definiteness and indefiniteness, saying: "His statement contradicts the consensus of the Basrans and the Kufans, so no attention is paid to it. The ruling of ʿaṭf bayān with the Kufans is the ruling of the adjective, so they make an indefinite follow an indefinite and a definite a definite, and Abū ʿAlī al-Fārisī followed them in that. As for the Basrans, it is not permissible with them except that both be definite, and it is not permissible that both be indefinite. Everything the Kufans brought that suggests the permissibility of its being ʿaṭf, the Basrans made a badal, and no proof has been established for the Kufans." I say: this question will come, if Allah the Exalted wills, in a thorough treatment at His saying, the Exalted: {مِن مَّآءٍ صَدِيدٍ} [إبراهيم: 16] and at His saying, the Exalted: {مِن شَجَرَةٍ مُّبَارَكَةٍ زَيْتُونَةٍ} [النور: 35].
When al-Zamakhsharī gave the i'rab of "the Station of Ibrāhīm and the security of whoever enters it" with the interpretation mentioned, he raised an objection against himself with what I mentioned about substituting a non-plural for a plural, and answered with what has preceded. He also raised an objection against himself as to how a clause could be an explicative apposition of single nouns, and said: "If you say: how did you allow «مقام إبراهيم» and the security to be an ʿaṭf bayān, when His saying {وَمَن دَخَلَهُ كَانَ آمِناً} is a resumptive clause, either an initial or a conditional one?
